orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, finishing her story for Lockwood. Cathy has just been taken to live at the Heights with her sick husband Linton, and Nelly is shut out, so most of this chapter is Zillah's account of the autumn of 1801, retold by Nelly. After the row of asterisks the frame returns to Lockwood's diary in the present: the winter of 1801–02, now the second week of January, and Nelly's story has caught up with him.

notes.g: Young Catherine (Cathy), now married to Linton Heathcliff.
notes.n: The household calls her 'Mrs. Linton' after her husband's first name, and also 'Mrs. Heathcliff'. Don't confuse her with her mother, the first Mrs. Linton, who died eighteen years ago.
Joseph's word, a common northern dialect form of 'throng'.

notes.t: who was dead and who living
notes.g: Who had died and who was still alive.
notes.n: Nelly means she is cut off from all news of the Heights.

notes.g: Nelly's affectionate name for Cathy, whom she raised.
Cathy: the wife of Heathcliff's son Linton.
Agreed; went along with it without protest.

notes.t: enlisted my informant among her enemies
notes.g: Turned Zillah, Nelly's source of news, into her enemy.

notes.n: A Scots and northern word.

notes.g: Shortly before Lockwood arrived in Chapter I.
notes.n: So Nelly heard this news in the late autumn of 1801.

notes.g: Came into the main living room.
notes.m: At the Heights the big family room is called 'the house' (see Chapter I), not the whole building.

notes.g: A quarter of a penny: the smallest coin there was.
notes.n: Heathcliff plays on the word: Linton's life is worth nothing, so he'll spend nothing.

notes.t: I cannot tell how to do
notes.g: I don't know what to do.
Play the nurse; look after him yourself.
Complained and was restless and miserable.
Would gladly; would have liked to.
Mr. Kenneth, the local doctor from Gimmerton.

notes.m: A servant's 'place' was her position or job, not a location.

notes.g: Terribly; so badly I nearly lost my mind.

notes.t: the only bell we have, put up on purpose for Linton
notes.g: A bell rung by a cord from the sickroom to call a servant.
notes.n: Big houses like the Grange had bells in many rooms. The Heights is an old farmhouse and has just this one.

notes.g: She said nothing; she was silent.
notes.m: 'Dumb' meant unable or unwilling to speak, not stupid.

notes.g: Linton is past suffering, and she is released from nursing him.
notes.n: She means Linton has died. 'Safe' because nothing can hurt him now, Heathcliff included.
Joseph despised Linton as a weakling.

notes.g: Linton's death (a polite way of putting it).

notes.n: Still common in Britain, rare in America.

notes.g: The legal document saying who gets Linton's property after his death.
Left to someone in a will.
Personal property such as money, furniture and goods, as opposed to land.
notes.n: Under the law then, a married woman's personal property became her husband's. So what had been Cathy's was Linton's to leave, and he left it all to Heathcliff.

notes.t: her week’s absence, when his uncle died
notes.g: The week Cathy was kept prisoner at the Heights while her father Edgar lay dying.
notes.n: See Chapters XXVII and XXVIII. Edgar was Linton's uncle.

notes.t: The lands, being a minor, he could not meddle with
notes.g: Because Linton was under 21, he couldn't legally leave land in his will.
notes.n: A 'minor' is someone not yet legally an adult, which then meant under 21.

notes.t: in his wife’s right and his also
notes.g: Probably: through his late wife Isabella's family claim, and as Linton's father.
notes.n: Nelly isn't sure this is legal. But Cathy has no money to fight it in court, so Heathcliff keeps the land.

notes.g: The main meal, eaten around midday.
Dressed in black: mourning clothes for her husband and her father.
As plainly as a Quaker woman wears her hair.
notes.n: Quakers, a Christian group, dressed very simply and avoided all decoration.

notes.g: A Nonconformist place of worship, outside the Church of England.
notes.n: In England 'church' meant the official Church of England; 'chapel' meant Methodists, Baptists and other dissenting groups.

notes.g: The church: here, Gimmerton's Church of England parish church.
Has no clergyman at present, so there are no services.
notes.n: So Joseph and Zillah go to the chapel instead.

notes.g: The meeting house of one of these Protestant groups.
notes.n: Methodism spread fast in Yorkshire in the 1700s. Emily Brontë's father was a Church of England clergyman.

notes.g: An older person keeping an eye on them.

notes.m: 'Nice' meant precise or refined, not simply 'pleasant'.

notes.g: Sunday kept holy, with no work, games or sport.
notes.n: Strict Christians thought shooting or even mending things on a Sunday was sinful.

notes.g: Oil from whale blubber, probably used here for oiling his guns.

notes.n: Still heard in Yorkshire: 'happen it'll rain'.

notes.g: Too refined and grand for Hareton.

notes.t: bring her pride a peg lower
notes.g: Humble her; take her down a peg.
That way; in the same direction.

notes.m: 'Humour' meant mood or temper, not comedy.

notes.n: Zillah calls Cathy the lady of the house, though without much respect.

notes.g: As proud and lofty as a princess.
A long wooden bench with a high back, set by the fire.
notes.n: The high back kept off draughts.

notes.t: he was sure she was starved
notes.g: He was sure she was frozen with cold.
notes.m: In Yorkshire 'starved' meant very cold, not hungry.

notes.t: I’ve been starved a month and more
notes.g: Cathy twists his word: she has been left cold and neglected for weeks.
notes.n: She stresses the word scornfully, as if to say: and whose fault was that?

notes.g: A kitchen cupboard with open shelves above for plates and other things.
She held out the skirt of her dress like an apron, to carry the books.
notes.n: A 'frock' is a dress.

notes.g: In such a state; so upset and agitated.

notes.s: Will you ask her to read to us, Zillah?
notes.tr: Will you ask her to read to us, Zillah? I'm sick of doing nothing; and I do like... I would like to hear her! Don't say I wanted it, but ask her yourself.

notes.n: Remember this word: Cathy picks it up in the next chapter.

notes.g: Show of kindness that isn't real.

notes.m: 'Society' here means company, not society in general.

notes.t: I never missed such a concern as you
notes.g: Sarcastic: 'Someone like you is no loss to me.'
notes.n: 'Concern' is a scornful word for him, as if he were a thing.

notes.g: Let me sit up through the night with Linton in your place.
notes.n: To 'wake' was to stay awake watching over the sick or dead.

notes.g: Taking his gun off his shoulder strap.
The gun work he had put aside because it was Sunday.
The hard winter frost had begun.
Lower herself to sit with us.
notes.m: Here 'condescend' means to stoop below one's rank, not to talk down to someone.

notes.g: Anyone who loves her or even likes her.
Recoil and snap back, like an angry animal.

notes.t: as good as dares him to thrash her
notes.g: Practically challenges him to beat her.

notes.m: 'Situation' meant a servant's position, not circumstances.

notes.t: set up Hareton in an independent house
notes.g: Give Hareton a home and income of his own.
notes.n: Heathcliff keeps Hareton dependent on him, as a farm labourer in what was once his own family's house.

notes.g: Fall within my responsibilities; be my business.
notes.n: Nelly's hint that Cathy might remarry is aimed at Lockwood, a single gentleman. Keep it in mind.

notes.g: Nelly's story has now reached the present day.
notes.n: From here we are back in Lockwood's own diary.

notes.g: Kenneth's prediction that Lockwood wouldn't be out of doors till spring.
notes.n: See the start of Chapter X.
Lockwood first visited the Heights in late 1801 and has been ill ever since.

notes.g: Heathcliff, who owns Thrushcross Grange and rents it to Lockwood.

notes.t: another tenant to take the place after October
notes.g: Someone else to rent the Grange once Lockwood's one-year lease ends.
notes.n: A 'tenant' rents a property from its owner.

notes.t: I would not pass another winter here for much
notes.g: I wouldn't spend another winter here for anything.
